segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We are going to talk for little bit. My name is Guy Soldier, but my real name is Richard. I don’t know where I got the name Guy, that’s just what they called me growing up.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Ohhh, what’s your name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know, maybe that might be it? Guy, I think. Because the old people used to call me Guy when I was growing up. The White people used to call me Guy, too. They called me Guy on both sides.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What’s your name in English?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Shirley Reed is my name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Shirley Reed. How ’bout in Cherokee, what’s your name?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Etsi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, my father, I didn’t know his last name. I didn’t know that he, Cherokees, didn’t have a last name. But his name and last name is Eli Dick, was his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Eli Dick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Eli Dick.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And that when White people say his last name it’s Ah Valvo.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ah Valvo? What’s the meaning of that?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I really don’t know. That’s just what they said, “That’s your last name.” But what I knew, that was it. But it all started, that, where my dad is from, around Cookson area.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Around Cookson.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, Cookson—where he grew up at.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was there a lot of Cherokee living around Cookson area at that time?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I think so. Reason why is because my dad was the oldest. I don’t know how many of them they were, because his mom has some boys. And, their dad, when he was going to town, and the car they were driving—their tires went flat. And they got out to fix it. And the car fell on top, and then my father ran really fast. Reason why is food was really expensive. He was making very little money, he was only making like 50 cents a week, was all he was getting paid. And that’s what they were buying—flour, and sugar. And they were buying stuff like that. And he took all that stuff out. And his father was laying there, dead. And he ran to the house and told his mom what happen. That—I guess he had to become a man. Because he was just a young boy at that time. He was a hardworking man all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess it wasn’t good money, back then, if they were only getting paid 50 cents a week.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, for long, that, because that. Wait, I don’t know what Cherokees call them. Korea—he used to be in the military. He didn’t even speak English when he came here. And, when he went with them, that’s where he learned English. And the numbers—he didn’t know them, and he learned that, too. Yeah, that’s what he did. And he was a good lookin’ man. He was real short and they say I take after him or look like him. Uh, I’m not telling you I’m beautiful, but how not-very-tall I am.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Don’t be saying that, because you are beautiful.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But he really liked to play music.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And he always played the guitar, and they would be dancing around. I guess that’s where him and Mom found each other somewhere. Because, my mom, she was around from Nicut area—that’s where she lived. I guess that’s where they found each other. My mom was on a horse, and he said he seen a beautiful lady. That’s when he wanted to be with my mother. He already had a woman, but they weren’t married, it was just his girlfriend. And that’s when they started fighting over my dad. Used to be. Mom said that she was on a horse, and the girl threw her off there… But I don’t know if that’s true or not, that’s just what she was saying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, they started fighting over him, right there?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, and that lady lived right by the house, too. Sometimes they will get into it when she brings that other lady up…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you live around that area that you’re talking about?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s where… now that I think about it, I don’t know what happened, but—that thing they call oil rights—that’s what my grandma had here. But I don’t know what’s happening. They used to live in a big house. Well, there was a big building—they used to be well off. And Mom said she would go to Sallisaw ’bout week at a time. And he would go get money. Somewhere over there, where he was getting paid for the oil rights. And, around that time, when that old lady passed away; that’s when things got bad for us, he said. And then their house burnt down. But you know the Indians that were given land? My grandpa was an Eagle, he had land. And that’s where they built a house, like they used to do a long time ago, when they build houses. I remember a little bit, what they used to do—kinda like glue and wood. That’s what kind of place we lived in back then. But then when my father find out, and—he wanted to be a better man, but, another reason, for his kids. And, when them Indians get sent off to work; he became a member of one of them, so then he was always working on road construction. He said they said he was really smart, a long time ago. And that’s what he did while we was growing. I guess we were well off, but in my mind we were poor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like what you’re saying ‘relocation’—they would take them somewhere and leave them.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Well, only some went to California… Whoa… If they would’ve took me over there, I wonder what would’ve happened to me over there? It’s really dangerous that way these days.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where is that at, you’re saying?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: California.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: California, that’s right.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s what they used to call it ‘California’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago some people called it a-de-l(a) de-ga-hl-dv. They said it that way. I guess that’s how it was back in the day. A lot of them went that way. But, at some point in time, I guess when it became… still, I guess it becoming more dangerous that way.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s right. You know—them people they call ‘brown corn’. I’ve never heard of them, but they were… men leaving, they would say, “They are going to ‘brown corn,’” they would say. My father would even go with them, sometimes. And another thing—it over there by Moffett Bottoms; it was pretty close there, and… what do they call ‘cotton’ in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh, wait a min… what do they call ‘cotton’? Do you know what ‘cotton’ is?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: We were at them cotton fields, picking cotton. Them things were pricking us hard in our hands. Inside the cotton, that’s what we used to do if we heard anything like that. They would pay us, when we did that like them Mexicans do nowadays. When they say ‘harvest to harvest’—that’s what we used to do. We would all fill up—we had trucks all the time, too; I don’t know where they were coming from—we would all fill up in the back of the truck.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s ’bout like when they pick those beans, when they were around, and strawberries.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s true. I don’t know if you had to pay quarter if you wanted to ride with someone. There was a man that lived by there that took them everywhere, and that’s what you had to pay.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember when I was a younger boy, I used to do that—I was picking beans.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, me, I was worthless. Because it was ten o’clock in morning, and I’d start throwing up, because I couldn’t stand the heat. I wasn’t worth anything, they didn’t want me going with them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you were just in the way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, where you grew up at, is that where you lived for ’long time?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what you’re talking about—that relocation. My dad went to Lincoln, Nebraska. And, then when we got out of school, my mom took us over there. Wait, there was three boys and three girls. We would go that way. And, when he got done working, in the wintertime, then we would go back this way. That’s what we were doing, and I been to that town. Me and my sister, when she was still alive, we would go to the movies. We would be walking around on foot. And, back then, all you had to pay was a quarter. That’s what we were doing. And other people, too, that live around there—they would show up. People that had kids, we would get together. All the old stuff they have called ‘museums’—we been to that. To see stuff like that I think is reason why I speak good English these days. I think, I learned there. But, my mom, she really wanted us to go to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You you all to learn English, yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But this is what they were saying, “Here this English book, y’all learn. And you come back in the house, you all are Cherokee” they told us. We never talked in English when we got inside the house. And also the elders, my mom and dad, we always talked in Cherokee, just like how we are talking now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, when y’all went over there, y’all would speak English. And when y’all came back, y’all were talking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: You know some people raised their kids, they said the white people were hard them so they don’t teach them any Cherokee, they just talk to them in English. But myself, I’m glad that it was given to me and taught me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My mom was a fluent speaker, also. And my sister and my brother, and we all spoke Cherokee. And all over—them ain’t living anymore. But, like I said, when I got home from school it was all speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: When my granny was still alive, she really has been all over the place; she came in here at the hospital because she had stroke.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She had a stroke.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: She had a stroke when the old building was there, she was here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That old building.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, she went in there. And we couldn’t get in for some reason. When we couldn’t go visit her, she took off walkin’ and came home. I don’t know what she did. She was crippled, I don’t know how. That’s what I think about sometimes, when I can’t do anything. And if I give up, I think, “My granny is crippled, and she walked all the way home.” That’s all I think about, but, that woman—she was a real Cherokee Indian. If she came to the hospital, and she seen White people in line in front of her, she would tell them to move. “I’m Cherokee Indian,” she tell them. She wasn’t scared of anything, she would say anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wonder what she would be saying now, if she came to hospital, and if you seen her there?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Whooo, she was scared to ride in the elevator. And myself, I’m a translator—I learned really fast to speak English, and they were dragging me around being translator. I was telling them, “I know a lot of things,” the other day. And, when I go in the hospital, the doctors, or nurses, telling what they are going to do to Indians. I know a lot of things that I’ve heard about. And some them I knew, they from up around Belfonte area. A lady—she was always letting kids out all the time. Her mind or thinking wasn’t very good. And she would do what them cows do, when they use a tree when the baby was coming out, and that what I heard them talking about. They say, “We are going to fix it,” they said. And, then they stopped, and got her to where she would have babies. I heard everything they were talking about, and they thought Indians didn’t know anything they were saying or talking ’bout, but I understood everything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s how it is.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But I got embarrassed to say anything… I got scared. I didn’t tell anyone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “This is what they going to do to me,” you thought. So, you got scared to say anything.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, I got scared.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout—are you still working?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m still trying. If I’m still good and if the Lord is willing me to, I told the kids I’m going to work. Wait—I have taught for over 30 years to this day. And that’s another thing, I made an effort to go to school, but I didn’t finish high school. But when I got married, I noticed—well Mom noticed, too—and she was pushing. And she told me, “You have to go to school,” she told me. So, now that place by the school, the men were watching me, because they knew I used to work there. I used to help the teachers. They told me, “You need to go to school, because you can make a good teacher.” And, really, just by them saying that, I became a teacher over here. And I would leave all the way over there, to here. And I thought about it—if I started in the summer, and I’ll finish next summer. I told myself, “Three years.” That’s how long it took me—three years. I don’t know if it was a week or two, then they hired me. I started working then. I started working at Moffett, and my granny did like it. She said, “Ohhh, Ahnigvnige—look, she going to teach them Black people.” That’s what they were saying, “Look at her, the one with a license,” they said. So then, again, we talked about it. I told her, “I’m getting paid more.” But I didn’t make that much more. But I told her, “They are paying me to teach.” She finally got to where she was OK with it. I worked there for 15 years. “She’s teaching over there, where them Black people are, and she is licensed to do it,” they were saying. And, then I started again, for the second time. This time it was a master’s degree. “How come you want another paper, you already have one?” she said. But I can’t make her understand. But Mom was OK with it, and said, “Well, at least somebody is learning.” Mom told me they came lived over here for little bit—here in Sequoyah. She said, “We lived here for little bit.” But Mom said they didn’t like it. They said they only stayed there two weeks, and then they brought me back.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, your mom was pushing you pretty good, for the better.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, then—it all just came back to me. I think that’s what they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She was just pushing you to get better, and that was what’s good about it.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And, my dad, all he did was work, that’s all he knew. He always told us, “You have to work,” he told us all the time. And, also, the-ones-that-are poor, their parents told us to work, too. They always told us not to make fun of them. “Because it’s not their fault,” they told us. We were the first ones to have a TV.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did people come over, that lived pretty close to y’all?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, it would stay on until ten o’clock… and then they would leave.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago, that’s what we used to do. His wife was a White lady—we used to know his wife—we watched boxing. And when they were fixin’ to start boxing—

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: —Oh yeah—

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: —he would have that TV sitting in the doorway, and we would watch the boxing from the outside. Or wrestling, that one wrestler they call ‘Bolo’.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Bolo.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you remember him?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: No… I didn’t really like that. But my dad used to like watching that. And, when he did, I went done other things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where you working at? Are you working here?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Wait.. I think it’s been 10 years since I been working here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Wait. I started at Moffett, and then Gore, and Brushy. And then I came here. I’m going to retire here soon, I think. I live right over there, where them elders live.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, where them little houses are?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Right there, where them Feelings live, that ‘Bendabout’, I say ‘Mrs. Bendabout’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, and them Russells.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, I think that One is sick, I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. Because when you get older your body starts going down.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah… my kids tell me that’s what’s going to happen to me. Because I don’t look for people to depend on. I like it better if I’m on my own. And I gotta teach them kids. They tell me, “You could be sitting all the time, and not do anything.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they told me—I had to settle down. Because I worked at the clinic in Jay for ’bout 30 years.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And when I retired there, I thought I was going to sit around.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: You didn’t like that?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My wife start wanting me to do things. As soon as I wake up, she would tell me, “This is what you need to do today.” But, you know, I got to thinkin’, “I guess she is doing good things for me,” I thought. And I’m able to get around. Because, really, if you sit around your body will go down also.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many kids did you say you had?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I have two kids. I have a girl, that’s the oldest—she is 57 years old. And my boy is 55 years old, I think. And that girl, I think she works at Stilwell CDC . And that boy, he retired from the Air Force. He is disabled, and they couldn’t fix it. They did surgery on him three times. Because he didn’t want to sit around not do anything, he told me, “If I can’t run, Mom, they won’t have me,” he said. So, he just retired.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did you say your parents’ name was, in English?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: My dad’s name is Eli Dick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Eli Dick.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I-Lo in Cherokee, and my mom was Odie Mea Eagle is her name, and in Cherokee is Sa-hoy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sa-hoy.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But they called her Wi-S-Si all the time. The reason why is because she loved hen-of-the-woods [du-wi-shi fungus].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ohhh, OK.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: They called her Wi-S-Si since she was a little girl. And them White people called her Bootsie.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Bootsie, oh.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Because she always had boots on, that were really tall, they said. But people that know her, they called her Wi-S-Si.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wishi, that was good eating, too.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Ohhh, she really loved them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m the Pastor over at the church in Kenwood. There was a young boy, but he passed on, and he would always ask for hen-of-the-woods. He would have it all cleaned up, all you had to do was cook it. And then he would bring me wild blueberries—wild blueberries. There was a lot, that way.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Nowadays, my kids tell me I’m not able to do it. My son, he knows a lot of them. He can recognize a lot of those plants. Myself, I can’t recognize them. Because he would say, “You can’t eat them,” he would say. “But you can eat these.” But I don’t know which ones they are. I never liked going outside, reason why—because it made me sick, throw up… I’d probably still do that to this day…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, your parents lived around there, where you’re talkin’—Belfonte area.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s where—

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: --that’s where they grew up.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. My granny was a Daugherty. Around Bell, I think. Because I really don’t know all the important things, I think. But, now, I want to find out about where my granny’s family is from. And my father is what they call ‘original enrollees’ there. Two of them, Israel, Eagle, are with me. And, thing they call ‘Lockman land’… Wait—my granny had about 150 acres, and then he gave it to his kids—and, whatever was left over, he gave it to me. At first, when I got married, my husband he was a young man. Well, I was young lady—we didn’t know anything. We were bouncing around trying find a place to live. We were renting, so this is what my granny said, “I’m tired of seeing you looking for a place to live. I’m going to give you some land” [unclear] And I said, “OK.” So now, as of today, there is a house there. And over this was… Callid lived there. I think it was because, so, she could watch me all the time. That’s who used to take me to church all the time, and I was a translator.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, you were helping the elders out a lot, translating.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I was going all over the place. And I didn’t know it, because I was just a little girl. But I would understand, and if I did, I would tell them. And that land that my granny gave me, we had to go to the courthouse. And she was sitting in a chair, and there was a judge on the other side. And they asked her bunch of questions. And he asked her, “Mrs. Lillia,” he said. He asked her everything. If he asked her if she understood it, she would say, “Haw, I understand.” And they were recording it, like we are doing here. And I thought to myself, “I wonder what I said,” I thought. “I understand,” she would say. That’s one thing—she was always scared. I asked Mom, “How come y’all are always scared?” I asked her. “Whenever y’all have to go in the judge’s office?” She would always be scared, too, still to this day. This past summer I got really sick. When I found out, I was really sick. So, I was giving the, my kids, the house. And everything I had in the house they put in the storage. And then I ended up having to go in there, and that—what the judge asked, “What is the reason we are doing this? Because you understand really good English, and you know what you’re saying,” he told me. “Old Indian Law,” he said, “They passed the law a long time ago,” he said. That’s what we did, and the paper is somewhere. I wonder where it’s laying around at.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, maybe it be on Muskogee somewhere?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. Because myself, I didn’t really get to know my granny either, when I was growing up. And she passed away, she had two sisters. And they told me, “You can call us granny,” they told me. So, I started calling both of them ‘granny’. And, also, when I was growing up, I just call both [of them] my granny. Because really, back then, they really loved one another. They never fought over anything, back then.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, nowadays, the kids will fight over everything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now I’m going to ask you this, but you don’t have to tell me if you don’t want. What do we call clans, Mitch?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Zu-ni-yv-wla.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, I was telling my boss—he’s a deacon at Park Hill. I don’t know if he still is. And my husband was a deacon also, at New Baptist. When we were members there. But I used to go to Stokes stomp grounds. Used to be, that’s where I would go. There were elders there, named Sa-hon. That’s where I would go, they would take me in on whatever they were doing. But in my real beliefs was where my husband’s was. That was it, that fellowship Baptist church. You seen it, haven’t you, that sign?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where is that at?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Over there, by where before you get to Anglen’s grocery store. Right there in Nicut, we have a sign there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it the one on the left side?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: When he first started at that church, me and my husband lived there. I didn’t know that the good Lord was going to take it over. So, we just thought he was going to start right there. But you know it was just given to us, so there wasn’t any reason why. I didn’t want anyone getting it. And people started coming and fillin’ up in the room. So, then we went outside. And then there, too, [it filled up]. So, then they said, “We gotta build it bigger,” they said. They looked for land everywhere. But it wasn’t working out, and I lived right next to it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Who is the Pastor there?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Ed Baker.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, I know him.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: A White guy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ed Baker, yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: He’s getting old on us now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, oh.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s where we all started. His wife, my dad and his wife, every one of us. And that’s when my granny gave them the land. And, there again, I went over there shaking. They told me I was the one that was going to have to ask for it. “Yoneg… Yoneg wants it. Yoneg is going to be a preacher. You know how bad it was when we was growing up. You’re the only one that can ask her for it,” they said. I thought about it real hard and read the Bible and talked to God. “Don’t be scared, don’t be scared.” But I was shaking when I went over there. She was sitting outside in her rockin’ chair. And, when you get there and if you look, you can see where we had a garden, me and my husband used to be. And there, where I was gonna ask her for that land. So, I told her, “Granny, can you give us some land that we can build a church on?” She thought about it real hard, she got real quiet. She was looking out there. I listen to her chair for ’long time. Her chair was metal. I told her, “We have a Bible school at my house.” And she said, “Your house ain’t big enough.” She was lookin’ that way, “Yeah I’m going to give it to you,” she said. “Reason why is because my kids and grandkids are going to come here,” she said. “You’re going to teach them here. Y’all are going to teach them here,” she said. “What they need to believe in and everything like that,” she said. And that’s really what happened. Pretty much all of my family became members there. And then, some of her grandkids that were lost—they came back.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, man.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And then at some time, my uncle’s boy—he was doing all of the wrong things. I heard he was sick because he been drankin’, but I knew. That’s where I taught him at; he became a believer, and he got baptized there at the church. I always thought about him. Then it finally hit him in his heart, and that boy passed away. But he was like a one-child and parents let him go. If my granny and my mom was alive, he wouldn’t be that way. I guess he would been sick in the cold. What happen to him was really bad, and this is where he passed away. And that’s what I think about, how he would think real hard. And he would see Jesus, and then me, I’d be shaking. That’s what I was telling my granny. We used to call her ‘ma’am’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your granny used to be… Y’all called her ma’am?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, all of us did… and she thought, you know, when White people say, “Yes ma’am,” that’s what she thought, that’s what they meant…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: She said, “How come they know my name?” she said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If they said, “Yes ma’am,” she thought they were saying her name.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, “They know my name, how do they know my name?” she would say.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, it was amazing. I used to visit her all the time, and see her rockin’ in her rocking chair… and I’d be sitting there, [her] telling me stories. I think to myself, “I wish I would’ve listened.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You would know a lot of things.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, I really would. I really do miss her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, your granny had been seeing it for long time, when you was asking her for that land.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, she was seeing it. And, myself, I wasn’t even thinking about anything. Because if I could do it, I would get it today. “I’m not sick today,” or, “I’m not going to get sick.” That’s what we think about. But her walking with her belief was really strong.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your late granny, did they live around that area when they were growing up?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Well, what I know ’bout that is that… Israel, ‘I-sal’ they called him, he was only 36 when he passed away. Reason why, is that he had typhoid fever, killed him. And then, my granny when they say ‘sleepwalkin’ [unclear] she was sleepwalking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they used to say to them, “There they go sleepwalking.”

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: They would say, “She sleepwalking,” like that. That’s what happened, they said. For little bit. “Why would I be doing wrong for what I’ve heard? Because God has already forgave me for what I’ve done, or what I said.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true. How ’bout, who was it, was it your late mother that you were saying that she was on a horse? [unclear]

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Then, she threw her off the horse, because she was mad at that lady. She said she threw her off the horse. I don’t know if she really did that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s when they got to know each other [your parents].

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s when.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: My late mother was very beautiful.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: They say my granny is part White. But, ohhh. You ain’t going to say that to my granny. If you tell her she was part White, she probably beat you up I think. They used to say she had brown hair and blue eyes, and that’s why they said she was part White. But nobody would say it to her face.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was she speaking English? Was she speaking all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you said.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: She understood English a little bit. Like they say—jumping around. But, I was her translator, if she went to the doctor or if she was sick. Sometimes we rode the bus, we went to Sallisaw, I didn’t know…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. It was always good to have someone around that could translate. Because, when I used to work at the clinic, there were a lot of elders living. But most of them have passed on. And, sometimes if they asked them, “Do you understand?” they would say, “Yeah,” but they really didn’t understand. And, when they seen me, they would come to me and ask me, “Can you look at this? What we have to do to take these pills?” And when I tell them they would say, “Ohhh, now I understand.” Because if they are Cherokee, if they ask them if they understand, and they say ‘yeah’, but they really don’t.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I wonder why we are like that. Whenever I got here, I’m going to tell you again, we didn’t have a place to put trash in. So I asked Mrs. Bendabout, “What do you do with old stuff?” And she said, “My daughter hauls it off somewhere.” So I asked Russell, he said, “Whenever we go home, we stop and throw it away.” So I thought about it, so I asked Micheal. He said, “This way.” I told him, “I ain’t going to go that way,” I told him. “So I just go throw it away at the school.” We ain’t supposed to, but since we don’t have trash bins to use ourselves. But I don’t know how many times I’ve told Howard. And, now, they got right there by the door. I told them, “Hawww,” I said. “They put it by my door,” I told my daughter. “It’s sitting right there.” But now—we have one now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So y’all have one now?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. One time, one of the higher up said, “If you’re full blood Cherokee, if you’re full blood Cherokee,” he said. If he went to work somewhere, you know the ones that play ball, like softball. If they can’t hit the ball the second time, it’s the same way. If a full blood Cherokee, if he goes lookin’ for the third play and misses, the third time, he gets out. It’s the same way if a full blood Cherokee goes to look for job. Sometimes that’s going to happen to you, but don’t ever give up. That’s the same way way they did to you.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. If you think about it, a lot of things. That’s where everything goes and happens, and that’s things are happening today I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. That’s true. Because myself, too, I’ve struggled, too, in my past. Reason why is because I’m a full blood Cherokee. But this what I was told one time, “Guy, if you can find a job somewhere. Even if they pay you two dollars on every little thing you did. You still have two dollars more.” So, I really thought about it, and I thought, “Well that’s true,” I thought. Sometimes I worked where they paid me just a little bit. But, sometime along the way, it was more and more, like what you’re saying. That’s what you did, too.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. Thank you!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. You wasn’t giving up. But really, you would’ve gave up if you wanted to, but you didn’t give up.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I’m surprised that I really wasn’t worried about anything. Being human, for me to like myself—because my God made it beautiful. Not me, but God did. I say it all the time, “It’s not me it’s God.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what I do. I give it to him for everything to go good for me and my wife. And we give all the glory to God. It would be good if all the Cherokee would be that way, if they would not give up, and be strong for the Lord, and give it all to Him.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Because there are some still out there that’s has given up. But like you were sayin’, you had someone that was pushing you, telling you to do that. Or telling you how to do things. Because there are some out there that don’t have people like that. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout your last name, what was your last name again?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Reed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Reed. Where did that start from?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: When me and my husband got married? I don’t know about him either. Because it came from his mom’s second marriage. They had kids. My husband said they came from somewhere in Arkansas. But they really didn’t know, because he was an older man when he got with him and his mom. And he passed away when my husband was about 16 years old, my husband said. There is a lot of things he didn’t know about, same as me. But back then we thought we knew everything. I’m sure there still a lot of them that are still around, that are the same or alike, and they still care about me. Because just the other day his sister called me early in the morning. I thought, “Oh man, who passed away?” That’s what I thought. But it was her his sister, and she said, “I’m just checking on you.” She said, “I’ve been really thinkin’ ’bout you, you been on my mind. She told me, they still care about me. And I’m glad to this day that I told her that. “Y’all still love me,” I told her. She said, “Oh Shirley, you’re precious,” she said. They still treat me good. If they get together, they always tell me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And that was your used-to-be-husband,

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: He was a White man, Yoneg, not Cherokee. And then my granny was gripping around, too (going with White folk). She broke the blood, she broke blood, broke the bloodline.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, she got onto you for having a White man or married to a White guy.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But I was a translator, so that One had to take me with him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were they well off, your husband and his family?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: No. He was the same. We were both ’bout the same situation. We just did good when we grew up. Because he was a working man. And then, when I started going to school, and then working all the time, I had two or three jobs. And he was also doing good, too. We were doing good, living good together. And then he started going to dialysis, and then cancer, and then he passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be. So, he left a good last name for himself.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. My dad, too. Them Ones that own stores in Sallisaw, they always say, “There is not a better man than Eli Dick,” they would say. It’s really good. We got a good name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s good. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout, like I said my name is Guy, I don’t even know where that started. And then Cherokee call me Guy, and the Yonegs, the same like I said. How ’bout you, they never gave you anything, kind of other names? Sometimes they give other names, or they give you a name. Usti or then they would name someone Zu-gv-lu-d. Or they would take up on that name. You don’t have any kind of name like that?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: ‘Beeb’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Beeb is your name?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And them White people call me Speedy. Because they could say the name Beeb. But yeah, they said ‘Beeb’. But before Mom passed away, she didn’t want to be alone. We were always sitting around with her. If I went to the bathroom, or in the kitchen, she would say, “Beeb, Beeb…” She would barely be sayin’, “Beeb… Beeb, Beeb.” Then she would yell really loud, until I ran right to her then. But I would hear her say that. I still hear her calling me that, sayin’, “Beeb.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wonder what the reason was they called you ‘Beeb’?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I think it’s because when they say ‘bebe’, I think that’s where it started. I don’t know, because my granny always used to call me that, too. And, still to this day, I have two aunts that are still living—80 and 90 years old—and they call me that, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be. They haven’t forgot about it.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: No. And them White people, too, that are still around. And they will say ‘Speedy’. My daughter will tell me, “Well, that’s not you.” She will say, “You’re not Speedy, Mom,” she says.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout where you came from—you never heard anything exciting that they told you or anything?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: No. That’s the only thing—that at church, where it all begin. And how God used me. And I was the bookkeeper at church, and I would write stories. Walking with God. A lot of people used to like to look at it. I used to hear people, and whenever I quit, that’s what I’m going to do. Because I’ve already started.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, you have already started?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I’ve been talking to God. Even if it’s in the morning if I’m talking to Him, I’m always smiling. I always ask, “How come you’re always smiling?” I ask. He says, “Because you make me,” and I tell, “Look how crazy I am,” I tell Him. I just laugh at myself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m the same way. When I wake up in the morning, I’ll be talking to God. And then my wife will say, “What did you say?” I tell her, “I’m not talking to you.” Then someone was tellin’ me, one time early in morning, I guess I was sleepwalking. I was washing my face, He said, “Lord I don’t want to go to work today,” he said. I was just sitting, washing my face. I was sleepwalking. He told me later on that day. That’s what I was saying, he said. My Lord didn’t want me to go to work.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: You were too tired.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I’ll tell you another thing. Whenever I got here—my aunts are really scared. And whenever I got here, they were really scared. Myself, I haven’t ever been scared of anything. Sometimes I’ll notice things, and then I’ll just walk by and talk to God, and tell Him, “There is something strange in here.” I tell Him, “Get it outta here. Throw him in the pig pen,” I tell Him. That’s what I say. And if I do that, then everything will be good again.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what happens to me sometimes. And when that does happen, I just pray to God. “If there is anything that’s not good in here, remove it,” I tell Him. “Throw it in the water. Throw it as deep as you can, so it won’t bother anybody.”

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Sin, sin. They say that’s where it is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, it’s pretty amazing how the good Lord works,

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout your relatives or your parents, your grandma that came from North Carolina, they ever told you anything about that?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Their relatives—when they left there, when they ran us out of there to come this way?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah, they talk about it. They were already living when they were here, but they didn’t come from that way. I don’t know where they came from. But a lady, and an old lady, lived there. Her name was Lucy, that one right there. That’s where she came from when she was little, they said, all the time. And they took me with them, and I talked to that old lady. And the ladies… how would you say it, ‘carry’?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were holding things.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Right. Here, where they were wearing a dress, that’s where they were laying them down, they said. So, when one got tired (carrying) the shells, other lady would do same. And that’s what she was doing when she got here, she said. Because all the same as here was around anymore. That’s what happened and them ladies. That lady always had something exciting to talk about, but she passed away. I talked to her one time, that lady.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. She remembers things that had happened in the past.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Aww… My late granny, she always said, “We better be walking together sometime,” she would always tell us. So, when they started building those houses, she said, “Nope, not me. Because they aren’t going to take it from me,” she said. And I was the one sitting there in the new house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You know that place, I don’t know—that Long Perry—if you have ever heard of it? That’s the church they call ‘Long Perry’.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When they had it—the Lord and Savior ceremony, the Lord’s supper—the Ones that lived that way, that used it, it came all the way over here. And when they brought it here, they didn’t use it for a second time. It was very important. Now I think they still have it these days, from North Carolina. Because really, at that time, a long time ago, it wasn’t. Nowadays the Lord’s supper works how it works—they just use them little cups, they pour them in there. Back then they just used a big jug, and they would drink it, one at a time, and then bread. It was like that, they brought it over here because that was the old way, they still have that, I think.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Long Perry.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to call it ‘Long Perry’.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Which way is that at?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You know where—Little Kansas, that road when you get there. And then you go south, and then ’bout five miles or maybe not that far. On the left side, there is a store where they sell cigarettes. By the road there is a driveway, right by there, on left side and that’s where their church is.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Ohhh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. I don’t know, but it was really good, really pretty there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ’bout you, you don’t know anything that’s started from there?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: No. That’s the only thing is—when I talked to that lady one time. That’s the only thing I know, and then she passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But then, my granny wanted me to see this lady because they knew that she was from around that way. But then they said she was real little, they said, when she got here, from that way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This is what I’m going to ask you now. What do you think about some of these groups, and this school teaching Cherokee at this school that’s here? What do you think about it, do you think that’s a good thing that you see?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. The reason why is—that church I was talking about when I was in their fellowship—well, that’s where I still go, to church there. A preacher came there, and him, you might know him—John Hummingbird?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: You know that them syllabary, that make sounds? I hand them on the wall. He didn’t know them, he didn’t know them. “I have never learned to read that,” he said. And I try to teach my momma, because I want her to learn. And we would start here [unclear] “No mom.” That’s all she knows. Right here, the very last thing I tell her, “a…e…i…o,” that’s all she knew. And you’re not going to argue with my mom, no! But at the same time, it was what I needed to use to learn my language, and I respect that. Really, that’s what I believe—that. And I’m still glad that I’m still speaking the language, and learning to read. And me teaching. But I’m going to tell you this, I haven’t said it to anyone else. My late granny, or my mom, the people that call themselves ‘translators’—if they start talkin’, they said, “It’s like a slap in the face.” They said, “They are not sayin’ the right things,” that’s what they said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Because really, they sound things out different.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah. Some of the words they say are messed up. And then if you try to have a conversation, then they get lost.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: That’s what happen just yesterday, when we was in a room just right over there. There was a guy that came and sat down, and he was a ‘Master Apprentice’. That’s what he is there. We listened to him, so I thought, “I’m going to test him,” I thought. He started out real good, uh huh. He said—and he was just throwing words around really, at first—but when we started a good conversation. He would ask me what I said, “What did you say, who, or what did she say?” So now he was sitting there, worried. Like, what I’m sayin’—there is nothing wrong with (that), because they do want to learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah—if they really want to.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But, at first, I think they should get in groups. Really, just them and a Cherokee speaker. Because them ladies from Belfonte were in there, see, because they’re all native, like, over there, they are [all first language speakers]. And—where I live at or grew up at, it’s on White people side. And them [the first language speakers from Belfonte], if they go in the house, that’s what they are speaking [Cherokee]. What they used to do, a long time ago—that’s what they are still doing. And they—when me and them ladies talked about things, we were talking about medicine, and some were using the words that I didn’t know about. That’s the first time I’ve heard those words-that-they-used-’long-time-ago. So, I told them we need to sit down and talk. Because this is first time I’ve heard these words; because I’ve never heard anyone saying those words. That’s the only thing that I believe in—it’s a little aggravating. But my granny she didn’t like it, she would say, “They are tryin’ to speak broken Cherokee language,” she said.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: And them White that live over that way, I don’t know if you know them. But some of them speak really good Cherokee, and you can talk to them really good. And that One that was here yesterday, he’s a speaker—I think he was an Ojibwe Tribe— I really couldn’t understand what they were say very good… but it was like how we are talkin’. It was going, it wasn’t broken or anything. That’s the only thing I can say about that. But again, I respect what they are doing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, the ones that are learning... a long time ago we went to school together, a White person. He learned how to read the Cherokee language, but he didn’t know what he was saying. He could read it pretty good, but he didn’t know what he was sayin’. All he could do is read it, but didn’t know what the meaning was. Like you’re saying here them teaching Cherokee, if they would tell them what the meaning for the words are, or tell them, “This is what it’s called or meaning is”, but that’s what they are doing, ain’t they?

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Yeah… there are two of them that just started. It’s their first time. I don’t know if it’s two weeks or two months that they went to a White school and they are Indian kids. a girl and a boy. They don’t understand anything... numbers and we are way ahead. We are almost done and this little girl... I felt sorry for her. If I tell her to write it down and I look, I wouldn’t see anything written down. She went like this and wouldn’t write anything down.[unclear],I told her, They don’t understand.” I told her. “I’m going to have to teach them,” I told her. And that boy was sitting over there, he said, “Teacher, no English,” he said. I don’t and then I had to go back and tell them, “This boy don’t understand.” But then again... I have to say it in English... I told him. So then on your way here I was saying something to the kid… no Cherokee he can’t understand it. But they know it. We say it to them all the time, but when you have to speak this language, it is hard all the time. That’s the first thing I ask them all the time. “Does anybody in your family speak Cherokee?” But they will say no. And that’s where they lose it. There has to be someone that speaks Cherokee that will be standing right there that’s going to have to teach the kid. And we can’t be with them all the time. We can just do the best we can. That’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s all we can do. It’s really good that they are them so when they get out like, for instance, on the Cherokee side, then they will be able to speak it even just a little bit.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: But then an English teacher said this one day, she said my immersion students are the best performers, that’s what happening all the time, they have to... some of them are speaking three languages. There are some Mexicans in here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: I told him, “You don’t know, but you’re a smart kid,” I told him. I tell them that all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Because there are some that has Mexicans and kids. Yeah, well, I’m glad that we were able to talk.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: How long did we talk?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Over an hour, that’s good.

segments.speaker: shirley-reed
segments.translation: Look, I went past it.
